title: From without to within
hookLine: Lalla: my teacher gave me one teaching, go from without to within
tomorrow: Lalla searched far and wide. where did she finally find it?

lines: HIS MOM, ALONE IN A PEW.
cards: After the last guests left, Theo went back into the church for his jacket and found his mom alone in a pew, eyes closed, praying. He came out and told Zoe: that's just ritual.

Lalla would have something to say about that, and so would her neighbors. In one of her vakhs she says her teacher gave her a single teaching, only one: go from without to within. She took it as her whole rule of life.

teach.h: THE IDOL IS STONE, THE TEMPLE IS STONE.
teach.b: Lalla took it hard and far. In another vakh she turns on a temple priest. The idol is stone, the temple is stone, she says; top to bottom it's all one.
Whom are you worshiping, stubborn pandit?

teach.h: JOIN YOUR MIND TO YOUR BREATH.
teach.b: Join your mind to your breath. That's one side, and it's strong. If Shiva is the Self in every being, as her tradition teaches, then a stone image is not where he's kept, and the real worship is turning inward.
But Kashmir's Shaiva tradition held another side too, and it speaks just as clearly.

teach.h: ABHINAVAGUPTA: THE RITE IS A WAY IN.
teach.b: The Kashmiri teacher Abhinavagupta wrote at length on outer worship, puja: the offerings, the gestures, the sacred diagrams. For him and teachers like him, the outer rite isn't the opposite of the inner.
It's a way in. The hands learn what the heart doesn't know yet. A shared rite holds a family and a valley together, and it's there on the days you can't find the inside at all.
So here are both, at their best.
Lalla: don't mistake the stone for God; go in. The ritual teachers: the outer is a door, and you go in through it.
Back in the empty church, Theo's mom may have been doing both at once: a pew outside, and something turning inward with her eyes closed.

how: In Kashmir's Shaiva tradition, some practice centers on inner meditation, joining mind and breath, while puja, the outer worship with offerings and gestures, is kept at home and in temples as a way in.

games.q: what does “from without to within” mean?
o: Lalla's one teaching: turn from outer things to the inner
a Kashmiri custom of praying outdoors, then indoors
a rule to leave home and live in the mountains

games.q: two sides, one tradition: tap the pairs.
p: gave her one teaching: go within
told the idol and temple are stone
wrote at length on outer worship
the outer rite, as a way in

s: everyone in Kashmir's Shaiva tradition agreed that outer ritual is useless
teachers like Abhinavagupta wrote at length on puja as a way in to the inner.
Lalla says her teacher gave her only one teaching
go from without to within; she took it as her whole rule.
in her vakh, Lalla tells the pandit to worship a bigger idol
she tells him to join his mind to his breath.

games.q: you side with Lalla: go within. a friend who loves her temple's rituals asks for her side's best case. what's strongest?
o: the outer rite is a door: the hands learn first, then the heart
rituals are fine because everyone in the family expects them
rituals are where God is actually kept, so stay outside
games.why: that's the ritual teachers' case at its best: puja isn't the opposite of the inner; it's a way in.

practice: Start outside: rest your eyes on one thing in front of you, and look at it for a few breaths. Then close your eyes and let your attention follow the breath in, from the object to the air to the quiet behind it.

wordCard.voice: From without to within: the single teaching Lalla says her teacher gave her, and the rule she lived by.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: from without to within. Lalla goes straight in; the ritual teachers go in through a door. Second with Lalla and Mira.
